title: MA9-09305
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXXX, a Mexican citizen, aged 27, is claiming refugee protection in Canada under section 96 and paragraph 97(1)(b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

Mr. XXXX XXXXX stated that his life is in danger in Mexico because his former chief, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, delegate of XXXXXXXXXXXXXX of the state of XXXXXXX, and his accomplices, the drug trafficking group "Gran familia," as well as the federal police, wanted to kill him.
His problems began after he realized that his former chief, Mr. XXXXXXXX, had a relationship with the "Gran familia" cartel, and especially after he reported it.
The claimant stated that he entered the police training institute on XXXXX, 2007, and that he began working in XXXXX 2007.
On XXXXXXX, 2009, following anonymous reports, the claimant was mandated by XXXXXXXXXXXXX to investigate the goings-on in a building located in the XXXXXXX of the city of XXXXXXX, in Guanajuato.

The investigation revealed that the people who were entering the building were drug traffickers from "Gran familia," and that the investigators had discovered drugs there and had seized cellphones-many of the telephone numbers of these phones were registered to federal police officers, including someone by the name of XXXXXXX.
The claimant called one of these numbers and his chief, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, answered and asked him how he had obtained his private number.
The claimant responded that he had obtained it from the office of the public ministry because he had asked for it urgently, but his chief told him that no one at the public ministry knew this number.
Despite everything, the claimant wrote in his report that he had found his chief's cellphone number in the drug traffickers' cellphones.

On XXXX, 2005, the claimant was summoned by his chief, Mr. XXXXXXXX, who ordered him to stop the investigation and to destroy all of the evidence that he had accumulated, and he added that if he did not do it, he would have problems.

The claimant refused to obey his chief and, on XXXXXXX, 2009, he realized that his investigation file had disappeared. The next day, he made an appointment with the coordinator of the ministerial police station, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, and reported his chief, XXXXXXXXXXXX, and his federal police accomplices, as well as the "Gran familia" cartel. He alleged that he gave the only copy of his investigation to the coordinator, after telling him that his report and the proof found had disappeared.
The coordinator advised him to leave things as they were and, on XXXXX, 2009, the claimant received a threatening telephone call on his cellphone.
Once again, he went to the area coordinator, Mr. XXXXXX, who told him that he had many enemies, insulted him and beat him.
The claimant requested protection from the Office of the Attorney General, before the chief of the area's public ministry, who told him that he could not offer him any physical protection.

On XXXX, 2009, he went to the public ministry of XXXXXXX, where the officer did not register his report in a preliminary special investigation report because they were verbal threats and they did not constitute an offence unless physical assault was involved. That same day, four individuals in a pickup truck threatened him with a weapon and beat him. The claimant went to the clinic and then to the public ministry, where he reported the physical assault and submitted a medical certificate. He clarified, however, that he was not given a copy of the complaint.
On XXXXXX, 2009, his chiefs summoned him and the agent of harm and asked for his resignation.
On XXXXX, 2009, three masked men went to his home but he managed to get away from the house and went to XXXXXX. He applied for his passport on XXXXX, 2009.

On XXXX, 2009, four men tried to intercept him as he was getting into a taxi. Once again, he was able to escape and went to the public ministry, where he was told to limit his complaint to the incident that had occurred that same day.

The claimant took refuge in XXXXXXX, in the state of Mexico, but on XXXX, 2009, he was the victim of an attempted kidnapping by two people, and once again, he was able to get away. He returned to the public ministry and then went to Puebla.
On XXXX, he decided to leave Mexico and arrived in Canada on June 21, 2009. ANALYSIS Identity
The claimant's identity was established satisfactorily by means of his passport, which was seized by Citizenship and Immigration Canada (CIC). Credibility
The claimant's testimony contained numerous implausibilities and some omissions that undermined his credibility.

He testified that, in an investigation, he discovered that XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXX had connections with the drug traffickers of the "Gran familia" group and that, after he discovered this, he included this information in a report that disappeared from his office afterward.

When asked to explain whether XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX was his immediate superior, the claimant responded that he was the superior of his team chief, XXXXXXXXXX. When he was asked to explain whether he was alone on that investigation, the claimant responded that they were a team of XX police officers.

The claimant also testified that, when he wanted to check who the telephone numbers belonged to on the cellphones seized in the drug traffickers' home, he came across XXXXXXX XXXXX, who allegedly asked him how he had obtained his private number. The claimant allegedly told him that he had obtained it by making an urgent call to the public ministry, and the commander allegedly told him that the ministry did not have that number.

The panel considers it surprising that the claimant, who worked on a team of 15 people and who had a group chief, had taken the initiative to check the numbers seized without informing his chief. The excuse that the claimant allegedly gave to the XXXXXXX about how he had found his private number is completely unrealistic and implausible.

In fact, if a situation came up in which the XXXXXXX's private number absolutely needed to be obtained, it is likely that this would be the task of the group chief, who, according to the hierarchy, is between XXXXXXXXXXX and the claimant. It is also surprising that the order to check the numbers found was not given by the group chief and that the report and the evidence, which according to the claimant were stolen from his office, were not requested and held by the group chief.

The claimant also testified at the hearing that, after he discovered the ties between the drug traffickers and XXXXXXXXXXX, the XXXXXXX asked him to stop the investigation and the claimant refused to do so.

The panel is of the opinion that it is implausible that XXXXXXXXXXXX contacted the claimant to tell him to stop the investigation, when he could have simply asked the group chief, Mr. XXXXXX, to stop the investigation, since he was his hierarchical superior.

Furthermore, since XXXXXXXXXXX was XXXXXXXXXXXXXX superior, he could not ignore that there was an investigation under way into the building, and it is, at the very least, surprising that if he was tied to the drug trafficking group, he did not tell them to make the evidence disappear.

Furthermore, the claimant testified that the home that was allegedly searched belonged to the drug traffickers of the "Gran familia" group; when asked whether the home was guarded and to specify how he entered, the claimant responded that they had an arrest warrant. He then specified that he had carried out about ten inspections of the home and that he had checked each of the cellphones found and, when he called XXXXXXXXXXX, he told him that he was calling to give him the results of the inspection.

The panel is of the opinion that this explanation is not valid because there is no reason why the claimant, who had received the mandate from XXXXXXXXXXXX, would call XXXXXXXXXXX on a private number, claiming that he wanted to give him an inspection report.

Confronted with that implausibility and asked to explain how XXXXXXXXXXXX had reacted when he responded, the claimant stated, [translation] "He was surprised; I told him that I had asked for his number to fill him in on the investigation."

Furthermore, the claimant testified that he wrote an investigation report and that he kept it; he specified that the report was kept at the archives office. He also testified that his colleagues knew about the report but did not have a copy of it because they were busy with other investigations.

The claimant also testified that he had submitted a copy of the report, after XXXXXXX, to XXXXXXXXXXX, but that he had not given a copy to his group chief, XXXXXXXXXXX. He testified that XXXXXXXXXXXX demanded that he give him the report and that his copy then disappeared.
When asked to explain why he did not indicate in his Personal Information Form (PIF) that he gave the report to XXXXXXXXXXXX, the claimant responded that he did not know.

The panel is of the opinion that it is a significant omission that undermines the claimant's credibility in that it concerns an incident that is central to the refugee protection claim. In addition, the claimant's testimony about the procedure to follow for producing and archiving investigation reports was not clear or specific, and the panel does not believe that such an incident ever occurred.

The claimant testified that the chiefs asked him to resign and that he was a victim of several attacks and attempted killings. He also specified that he was followed and found in XXXXX and in XXXXX. When asked why his powerful enemies, that is, Police XXXXXXXXXXXX, the members of the "Gran Familia" cartel, and other police officers of the federal investigations agency (AFI) would continue to look for him everywhere, the claimant responded that he is a threat to them. He was also asked why these people would go to the trouble of looking for him everywhere because, according to his testimony, he filed a complaint against his attackers on a number of occasions and he went to see XXXXXXXXXXXX chief, XXXXXXXXXXXX, and all of this was unsuccessful; he stated, [translation] "it is because I am a threat to them." The claimant did not demonstrate that his powerful enemies have reasons to feel threatened by eventually being reported by him; the report and the evidence allegedly disappeared and all of his attempts to file complaints were to no avail.
The panel does not believe that this story is true.

After analyzing the testimonial and documentary evidence, the panel concludes that the claimant did not discharge his burden of establishing that there is a "serious possibility" that he would be persecuted on one of the Convention grounds. He did not demonstrate, on a balance of probabilities, that should he return to Mexico, he would be personally subjected to a danger of torture or to a risk to his life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment.
For all of these reasons, the panel determines that the claimant is not a "Convention refugee" or a "person in need of protection."

The panel rejects the refugee protection claim of XXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXXX.
